## Background

### The explosion of digital data

We live in an era of **mass production of digital data** (Digital Data Production). The volume of information created, captured, copied and consumed in the world is growing exponentially from year to year.

To give a concrete measure of this reality:

- In 2010, the world produced about **2 zettabytes** of data.
- In 2025, this quantity exceeded **180 zettabytes**.

A **zettabyte** (zetabyte) represents $2^{70}$ bytes, or **1 billion terabytes**. It is so large that it is difficult to intuitively design.

This growth is not linear but **exponential**: the amount of data doubles every few years, making traditional information management methods insufficient.

#### Why the explosion?

Several factors explain this growth:

- The democratization of **smartphones** and connected devices.
- The development of **social networks** (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X...).
- The digitisation of **public and private services** (health, education, banking...).
- The development of the Internet of Things (IoT).
- The generalization of **streaming** video and audio.

To remember: the amount of digital data available far exceeds the human capacity to process them manually. This is the raison d'être of the Information Retrieval (Information Retrieval).

---

### A digital world

#### Photography as an emblematic example

Photography perfectly illustrates the transition to an entirely digital world.

- In **1826**, the first photograph was taken: 0 billion photos per year.
- In **1930**, with the democratization of the silver apparatus, about **1 billion** photos are taken each year.
- In **2000**, at the peak of silver photography (Analog photos), this figure reached **86 billion**, before falling sharply with the arrival of digital technology.
- In **2011**, the total (digital + analog photos) exceeds **380 billion** photos per year.

This graph illustrates two important phenomena:

1. The **Technological rupture**: Silver photography collapsed in the 2000s, replaced by digital.
2. The** amplification effect**: by removing the marginal cost of shooting (no need for film), digital multiplies the volume of data produced.

The same logic applies to all forms of content: texts, videos, messages, audio recordings. Digital lowers the cost of production and causes a **information avalanche** (avalanche information).

---

### A connected world

#### What happens every minute on the Internet

The figures illustrating online activity are dizzying. Every **minute** on the Internet includes:

- **3.47 million** videos watched on YouTube.
- **625 million** videos viewed on TikTok.
- **3.5 billion** Snaps created.
- **66,000** photos and videos shared on Instagram.
- **350,000** tweets sent.
- **231 million** e-mails sent.
- **6.3 million** Google searches.
- **44 million** people watching Facebook Live.

These figures highlight the ubiquitous need for research and access to information** in our daily use. Research alone accounts for 21% of the time spent online.

To be remembered: Global connectivity is constantly generating new content and access to information needs. Information Retrieval systems are at the heart of this infrastructure.

---

### A Changing World

#### Continued growth of online content

The digital world is not stabilizing: it is constantly evolving, and this evolution is accelerating.

A striking example is **YouTube**:

- In **2012**: 30 hours of video were uploaded each minute.
- In **2024**: this figure is **500 hours per minute**.

It is a multiplication by **15 in 10 years**, illustrating the exponential acceleration of content production.

This poses constant challenges to Information Retrieval systems:

- Algorithms must adapt to ever-increasing volumes.
- The types of content are diverse (text, image, video, audio, structured data...).
- Uses evolve (voice search, multimodal, contextual...).

---

## Motivation: user needs

### Understanding user needs

#### How people spend their time online (2012)

In 2012, studies on Internet use revealed the following distribution of time spent online:

- **22%**: Social Networking
- **21%**: Research (Seaches)
- **20%**: Reading Content
- **19%**: e-mails and communication (Emails/Communication)
- **13 %**: multimedia sites (Multi-media Sites)
- **5%**: Online Shopping

Thus, **nearly 41% of online time** is devoted to activities directly related to research and information consumption (research + content reading). Information Retrieval is therefore at the heart of digital usage.

---

### Major needs identified

#### Making informed decisions

**Decision Making is a fundamental need of users. Any decision—whether personal, professional or academic—requires access to relevant**, **reliable** and **up to date** information.

Without structured access to information, decision-making is based on incomplete or biased data.

---

#### Manage information avalanche

The information avalanche** (Information Avalanche) is one of the great challenges of our time. Being exposed to a massive volume of information does not mean being better informed: on the contrary, without suitable tools, it generates **cognitive overload** and **disinformation**.

It is therefore necessary to implement **Advanced Information Management Processes, capable of:

- Filter relevant information.
- Organize and structure content.
- Present information in an exploitable manner.

---

#### Access to large information depots

Access to **large information repository** is the foundation of **Data Science**. Machine learning, statistical analysis or data visualisation algorithms are of value only if the underlying data are accessible, represented and comparable.

To be remembered: Information Retrieval is a fundamental building block of Data Science because it makes data exploitable on a large scale.

---

### Bringing structure to raw data

To meet these needs, it is essential to **structure raw data** (Raw Data). This involves three essential steps:

#### 1. Appropriate Data Representation (Document Representation)

A raw document (text, image, audio, video...) cannot be directly compared or analyzed by an algorithm. One ** formal representation** must be extracted:

- For a text: a word frequency vector.
- For an image: a color histogram, or a vector of visual characteristics.
- For audio: spectral descriptors (MFCC, etc.).

The quality of this representation directly determines the quality of the following analysis.

#### 2. Appropriate Similarity Measurements

Once the documents are represented, you must be able to compare them **. **Measurements of similarity** (or distance) adapted to the nature of the data are defined for this purpose.

- Euclidean distance in a vector space.
- Cosine distance for term vectors.
- Distance from Hamming for binary data.

The choice of similarity measurement is crucial: a bad measurement leads to inconsistent results, even with good representation.

#### 3. Analysis process: search, learning, visualization

Once represented and comparable, the data can be subjected to **analytical processes**:

- **Data mining** (Mining): clustering, detection of abnormalities, frequent patterns.
- **Learning**: classification, regression, walking.
- **Visualization** (Visualization): reduction of dimensionality, similarity maps.

---

### The Information Management Pipeline

The general information management process can be summarized as follows:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Gross documents] --> B[Extraction of characteristics\nFeature Extraction]
    B --> C[Features\nDocument Features]
    C --> D[Appropriate mapping\nAppropriate Mapping]
    D --> E[Representation space\nRepresentation Space]
    E --> F[User Interaction\nUser Interaction]
    F --> G[Decision-making process]
    G --> H[Decision]
```

This pipeline is **universal**: it applies to texts, images, videos and any other type of digital data.

---

### Concrete examples

#### Example 1: Text documents

For a corpus of **text documents** (Text Documents), the pipeline works as follows:

1. **Extraction of features**: The occurrences of each word are counted in each document. We obtain ** terms frequency vectors** (Word Occurrences / Term Frequency vectors).

2. **Appropriate mapping**: a transformation (e.g. TF·IDF or dimension reduction) is applied to move from a hollow to a dense representation.

3. **Representation space**: documents are projected into a vector space where similar documents are close to each other — visible in the form of a **word cloud** (Tag Cloud) or thematic map.

4. **User interaction**: The user formulates a query, the system returns the most relevant documents.

5. **Decision**: The user has access to the information they need.

The notion of **word cloud** (Tag Cloud / Word Cloud) is a simple but effective visualization of the distribution of terms in a document or corpus.

---

#### Example 2: Images

For a collection of**images** (Images), the same pipeline applies:

1. **Extraction of characteristics**: **color histograms** (Color Histograms) are extracted for each image — a compact descriptor representing the colour distribution (red, green, blue).

2. **Appropriate mapping**: Histograms are projected into a representation space where visually similar images are close.

3. **Representative space**: The images are arranged in a 2D or 3D space according to their visual similarity.

4. **User interaction**: the user can navigate in this space, select a reference image, and get the most similar images.

5. **Decision**: result in the form of **photo collage** (Photo Collage) filtered according to the user's needs.

Color histograms are global ** descriptors**: they capture the colorimetric palette of an image, but ignore the spatial position of the colours. More sophisticated descriptors (SIFT, CNN features) capture more local information.

---

#### Example 3: Other types of media

Information Retrieval is not limited to text and images. It applies to:

- **Audio and video**: transcriptions, spectral descriptors, temporal characteristics.
- **Webpages**: hypertext structure, links, metadata.
- **Messages** (e-mail, chat): text content, temporal and social metadata.
- **Services and processes**: log systems, process states.
- **People, businesses, communities**: social graphs, user profiles.
- **Web 1.0** (static pages), **Web 2.0** (social networks), **Web 3.0** (Internet of Things / IoT), **Web 4.0** (metavers / verse).

To be remembered: any object to which **digital characteristics** may be associated may be subject to a Information Retrieval. Discipline is therefore **universally applicable**.

---

## Distance in Information Retrieval

### Distance: a central concept

#### Why is distance fundamental?

The concept of **distance** (or similarity) is at the heart of Information Retrieval. It answers a simple but fundamental question:

> *To what extent do two documents deal with the same subject? *

Distance is not only a technical tool: it is the **mathematical formalization** of the human intuition of resemblance between two contents.

---

#### The example of presidential speeches

To illustrate the problem of distance measurement, consider two clouds of words from State of the Union Address:

- **Speech by George W. Bush (January 29, 2002)** The most common words are *war, terror, terror, security,weapons, freedom, nation, people*.
- **Speech by Barack Obama (25 January 2011)** The dominant words are *jobs, business, future, education, governance, work, people, nation*.

These two speeches share common terms (*people, nation, country, jobs, work*), but their thematic content is **clearly different**: national security vs economy and education.

Two fundamental questions arise:

1. **How to measure this difference in a formal and quantitative way?
2. **How to tolerate variations** in style, language, vocabulary while capturing similarity of meaning?

These questions are not trivial. A "job security" document can simultaneously use the vocabulary of both speeches. A naive distance measurement (word count) is not enough to capture the semantic nuance.

---

### The omnipresence of distance

#### Distance applications in data analysis

The distance (or proximity / similarity measurement) is used in all major areas of data analysis (Data Science):

##### Unsupervised Mining

- **Clustering** (consolidation): group similar documents without prior labels.
- **Due to anomaly** (Outlier Detection): identify documents that differ significantly from others.
- **Imputation**: estimate missing values from nearest neighbours.

In clustering, two documents are placed in the same group if their distance is less than a certain threshold. The result depends entirely on the measure chosen.

---

##### Supervised Learning

- **Classification**: assign a category to a document based on distance to training examples (e.g. k-NN).
- **Regression**: estimate a numerical value (e.g. relevance of a document) by interpolating from neighbours.
- **Ranking** (ranking): order documents by decreasing relevance to a query.

---

##### Visualization

- **Dimension Reduction** (Dimension Reduction): Project high-dimensional data in a 2D or 3D space by preserving the distance between points (e.g. t-SNE, UMAP, MDS).

Visualization allows a user to **navigate intuitively** in a large documentary space, exploring thematic clusters.

---

#### The three roles of distance

Distance plays three distinct but complementary roles in Information Retrieval:

1. ** Characterize a document**: the characteristics (features) of a document form its numerical "summary" — what it is in itself.

2. **Compare two documents**: distance is used to quantify the **similarity** between two documents — their relationship to each other.

3. **Characterize a model of documents**: the distribution of distances in a collection allows to visualize the overall **structure** of the corpus — how the documents are organized between them.

---

## Definition and objective of Information Retrieval

### What is Information Retrieval?

#### Main motivation

**Information Retrieval** (Information Retrieval, IR) has as its main motivation ** to respond to an informational need** (Information Need).

An informational need arises when a user does not have the information they need to complete a task or make a decision. It then forms a **query** (Query) to access this information.

The challenge is to match an imprecise query (formulated in natural language, often vague) with the most relevant documents of a large corpus.

---

#### Formal definition

> The Information Retrieval consists of ** automatically emerging** information **relevant** from a **large collection of documents**, in response to a **query formulated in a flexible way** (loose query formalism).

Let us decompose this definition:

- **"Automatically emerge"**: The system must operate without human intervention for each query.
- **"relevant information"**: relevance is relative to the user's need, not just the presence of keywords.
- **"Large collection of documents"**: IR systems are designed to scale.
- **"Loose query"**: the user does not need to know the internal structure of the collection or to use a formal language.

---

#### The general framework of an IR system

A Information Retrieval system operates according to the following scheme:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Information needs\nInformation Need] --> B[Query\nQuery]
    B --> C[IR\nIR System]
    D[Document Collection\nDocument Collection] --> C
    C --> E[Relevant documents classified\nRanked Related Documents]
    E --> F[User\nUser]
    F -->|Feedback| C
```

The ** feedback** loop is important: the user can report what results are relevant, allowing the system to refine its results (Relevance Feedback).

---

## History of Information Retrieval

### Historical Chronology

Information Retrieval is a discipline that has more than 70 years of history. The main stages of its development include:

#### Origins (1950–1960)

- **1950** : **Calvin N. Moors** creates the term *Information Retrieval*. This is the official birth of discipline as an autonomous field of research.

- **1959**: **Hans Peter Luhn** (IBM) describes the **statistical retrieval: the idea of using the word frequency to measure the relevance of a document.

的 Luhn introduces the idea that the most common words in a document (excluding empty words) are the most representative of its content.

- **1960**: **Maron and Kuhns** define the first **probabilistic model** of the IR: a document is relevant with some probability, depending on the query.

#### The emergence of models and assessments (1960–1980)

- **1966**: The **Cranfield project** defines the first **evaluation measures** in IR: precision (precision) and recall (recall). These measures remain fundamental today.

The Cranfield project is the first to evaluate IR systems in a rigorous and comparative manner, laying the foundation for experimental IR research.

- **1968** : **Gerard Salton** publishes his first book on the system **SMART** (System for the Mechanical Analysis and Retrieval of Text) — one of the first operational IR systems, based on the Vector Space Model.

#### Marketing (1970-1990)

- **1972** : **Lockheed** launches **DIALOG**, the first **commercial online service** to access bibliographic databases.

- **At the end of the 1980s** the first IR systems were integrated into **software for PC**, making the literature search available to the general public.

- ** Early 1990s**: Lower costs of hard drives lead to a **revolution of information storage**: large amounts of text can be stored on personal machines.

#### The Internet Age (1990–2000)

- **1992**: **Westlaw** deploys the first probabilistic IR system at **large scale** in the legal field.

- **Middle of the 1990s**: emergence of **Multimedia Databases** — integration of image, sound and video searches.

- **1994**: **Internet and Web explosion** — the volume of documents available is increasing dramatically, imposing new IR solutions.

- **1995**: IR techniques become ** omnipresent** — the "Search" button is everywhere. Web search is becoming a daily activity for millions of users.

#### The era of machine learning (2000 to present)

- **Today**: **embeddings** from Machine Learning Embeddings are used for research. Models such as BERT, GPT or deep neuron networks capture the deep **semantic** of documents and queries.

A *embedding* is a dense vector representation of a document or a query, automatically learned from large amounts of data. It captures not only words, but also their meaning in context.

To be remembered: Information Retrieval has moved from a confidential academic discipline ( 1950s) to a pervasive technology (web search engines, recommendations, virtual assistants...). Models evolve, but fundamental questions — how to represent a document? How to measure relevance? — remain at the heart of the discipline.

---

## Content and objectives of the course

### Educational objectives

This course aims to gain an in-depth understanding of the foundations and modern techniques of Information Retrieval. Specific objectives are:

- **Understand basic IR models**: Boolean model, vector, probabilistic, neuronal.
- **Understand social recommendation** (Social Recommendation): collaborative filtering, recommendation systems.
- **Include Quality Measures: precision, recall, F-measure, NDCG, MAP.
- **To understand the specific properties of media** (Media Specification): text, image, audio.
- **Explore indexing techniques** (Indexing): Inverted index, data structures for quick search.
- **Discover data visualization** (Data Visualization): dimension reduction, interactive visualization.

This course is part of the continuity of **Data Science and Automatic Learning** (Machine Learning). It assumes familiarity with the basic concepts of linear algebra, probability and statistics.

---

### Detailed course content

#### Part 1: Vector embeddings (Embeddings)

This central part of the course explores different ways of representing documents in a vector space.

##### Divings (Sparse Embeddings)

- **TF·IDF** (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency): weighting terms according to their frequency in the document and their rarity in the collection.
- **Vector Space Retrieval (Vector Space Retrieval) model: document representation and queries as vectors in a term space.
- **LSI** (Latent Semantic Indexing): reduction of dimension by decomposition into singular values (SVD) to capture latent semantics.

Hollow embeddingss are thus called because most vector coordinates are null (a document uses only a small subset of the total vocabulary).

##### Probabilistic Retrieval

- Models based on the **probability of relevance** of a document relative to a query.
- **Model BM25** (Best Match 25): one of the most widely used variants in practice.
- **Language Models for IR.

##### Dense Embeddings

- **Neural Embeddings: representations learned from deep neuron networks.
- **Word2Vec**, **GloVe**, **FastText**: embeddings of words.
- **BERT**, **Sentence-BERT**: embeddings of sentences and documents.

dense embeddings capture complex semantic relationships that hollow methods cannot represent (synonyms, polysemia, context...).

##### Learning to rank (Learning to Rank)

- Supervised learning methods to order documents by relevance.
- Approaches *pointwise*, *pairwise*, *listwise*.

---

#### Part 2: Indexing

- **Inverted Index** (Inverted Index): a data structure that allows all documents containing a given term to be found quickly.
- Techniques to make the search **scalable**: compression, partitioning, distributed calculation.

Indexing is what makes it possible to search billions of documents in milliseconds.

---

#### Part 3: Evaluation of Information Retrieval

- **Precision** (Precision): proportion of returned documents that are actually relevant.
- **Recall** (Recall): proportion of relevant documents that have actually been returned.
- **F-measure** (F-Measure): harmonic combination of precision and recall.
- **NDCG** (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain): measure taking into account the position of relevant documents in the ranking.
- **MAP** (Mean Average Precision): average precision on several queriess.

The evaluation of an IR system in a rigorous manner is essential to compare different approaches and progress in discipline.

---

#### Part 4: Social Information Retrieval and Recommendation

##### Information Retrieval on the Web (Web Information Retrieval)

- The Web as a graph of related pages (hyperlinks).
- **PageRank** and ranking algorithms based on graph structure.
- Crawling, web indexing, spam detection.

##### Recommendation Systems

- **Collaborative Filtering: recommend to a user what similar users have liked.
- **Content-Based Filtering: to recommend items similar to those that a user liked.
- **Hybrid approaches**.

##### Social Network Analysis

- Community detection.
- Centrality measures.
- Dissemination of information in graphs.

---

#### Part 5: Media Specificity

##### Text Properties (Text Properties)

- Natural Language Processing (NLP).
- Tokenization, Stemming, Lemmatization, Stopwords.
- Statistical models of language.

##### Visual Information Retrieval

- Descriptors of local and global images.
- Search by image (CBIR - Content-Based Image Retrieval).
- Convolutive Neuron Networks (CNNs) for the extraction of visual characteristics.

##### Information Retrieval Audio (Audio Information Retrieval)

- Time and spectral descriptors.
- Recognition of music, speech.
- Acoustic prints (audio fingerprinting).

---

#### Part 6: Information Visualization

- **Manifold Learning: t-SNE, UMAP, PCA.
- Interactive visualization of large documentary spaces.
- Exploration and navigation in document collections.

The visualization of the information closes the loop of the IR pipeline: it allows the user to understand and explore the structure of the collection, and not only to respond to punctual queries.

## General references

### Basic Bibliography

The course is based on an authoritative set of references in the field. Here are the main ones:

#### General works in IR

- **Baeza-Yates & Ribeiro-Neto** — *Modern Information Retrieval: The Concepts and Technology behind Search* (2nd ed., 2011, Addison-Wesley). The classical reference, covering theoretical and practical foundations.

- **Manning, Raghavan & Schütze** — *An Introduction to Information Retrieval* (Cambridge University Press, 2009). Available online, very complete on classic IR models.

- **Croft, Metzler & Strohman** — *Search Engines: Information Retrieval in Practice* (Pearson, 2015). Focused on the practical implementation of search engines.

- **Büttcher, Clarke & Cormack** — *Information Retrieval: Implementing and Evaluating Search Engines* (MIT Press, 2010). Focus on evaluation and implementation.

#### Neuronal IR and embeddings

- **Mitra & Craswell** — *An Introduction to Neural Information Retrieval* (NOW, 2018). Introduction to neuronal approaches.

- **Tonellotto** — *Reading Notes on Neural Information Retrieval* (CoRR, 2022). Recent and accessible course notes.

#### Treatment of natural language

- **Jurafsky & Martin** — *Speech and Language Processing* (3rd ed., Stanford, 2026, available online). The essential reference for the NLP.

#### Recommendation systems

- **Aggarwal** — *Recommender Systems: The Textbook* (Springer, 2016). Comprehensive coverage of recommendation systems.

#### Text Search

- **Zhai & Massung** — *Text Data Management and Analysis* (Morgan Claypool, 2016). Unified approach to text search and IR.

- **Berry & Kogan** (ed.) — *Text Mining: Applications and Theory* (Wiley, 2010).

#### IR web

- **Ceri et al.** — *Web Information Retrieval* (Springer, 2013). Specific to the Web context.

#### Learning to rank

- **Liu** — *Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval* (Springer, 2011). Reference on supervised approaches to ranking.

#### IR algebra

- **Dominich** — The Modern Algebra of Information Retrieval* (Springer, 2008). For formal mathematical foundations.

- **Melucci** — *Introduction to Information Retrieval and Quantum Mechanics* (Springer, 2015). Unconventional approach based on quantum mechanics.

Specific references to each chapter will be provided as the course progresses. Bibliographic suggestions are welcome.

## Executive summary

### What to learn from this introduction

**Key points in this introductory chapter:**

Information Retrieval was born from a simple observation: the production of digital data is growing exponentially, and humans cannot handle this volume of information manually.

In response to this **information avalanche**, three basic needs are emerging: making better decisions, managing information effectively, and accessing large data repositories to make science.

To meet these needs, it is necessary to **structure the raw data**: to represent them formally, to define appropriate similarity measures, and to apply analytical processes (search, learning, visualization).

**Distance** is the central concept of Information Retrieval: it allows you to compare documents, group them together, classify them by relevance, and visualize them.

An IR system aims to ** automatically emerge the relevant information** from a large collection of documents, in response to a flexible query formulated by a user.

This course will cover classical and modern IR models, from TF·IDF weighting to neuronal embeddings, indexing, evaluation, recommendation systems and data visualization.
